newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Tight labor mkt a concern in US Jan jobs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Tight labor mkt a concern in US Jan jobs.

text.p: U.S. markets have already discounted another healthy month of payrolls gains and will be more vulnerable to fresh signs of labor market tightness when the Commerce Department releases its January employment report this Friday.

With an economy already teetering near full employment, economists said a solid advance in hourly earnings or a further decline in the jobless rate could change thinking at the Federal Reserve about the need for higher U.S. interest rates.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's veiled warnings about wage pressures in his recent testimony to the U.S. Senate have sensitized market participants to lingering tautness in the job market.

And although no change in interest rates is expected following the Fed's two-day policy meeting on Wednesday, the early reading on the central bank's intentions for late March will hinge in part on Friday's employment data.

"The thing that will be a catalyst for a Fed move over the next couple of months will be a further tightening of the labor market," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
"If the unemployment rate approaches five percent, even in the absence of any clear evidence of wage pressures, I think the Fed could step in and tighten."
Economists surveyed by Reuters are expecting the unemployment rate to dip back to 5.2 percent in January after a reading of 5.3 percent in December.
They are calling for a healthy nonfarm payrolls advance of 237,000 in January after a sizable 262,000 climb in December.

After jumping by a sharp 0.3 percentage points in December, the average workweek is expected to retreat from 34.8 hours to 34.6 hours in January. Growth in average hourly earnings is seen slowing to 0.2 percent in January after heady increases of 0.5 percent in December and 0.8 percent in November.
Economists noted that the trend in average hourly earnings has been on the rise, but that after two consecutive months of solid gains, a month of slower growth is expected.
The risk, they say, is that earnings post yet another month of sizable gains.
"The number that's clearly scary is anything above 0.3 percent," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc, referring to average hourly earnings.
Levenson expects payrolls growth of 260,000 in January, no change in the unemployment rate and a two cent decrease in hourly earnings.
"What we expect is to see strength in the headline but weakness in the details," he said. "I think the market would probably take some comfort in that after some initial shock."
But Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc, expects stronger details and a weaker headline reading showing 150,000 January job additions.
He said that a longer five-week survey period for January could pick up more layoffs than usual and depress the headline number.
Karydakis questioned however, whether hourly earnings growth would slow substantially, as is widely anticipated.
"We had two outsized back-to-back increases in average hourly earnings and one might think that it's about time we get a below-trend number," he said.
"But we're also in a period where the trend is moving higher," he added, noting that his forecast is for a 0.3 percent advance.
Karydakis agreed that a sizable decline in the unemployment rate represented the biggest risk, predicting that a reading of 5.1 percent would be particularly worrisome for financial markets.
"That would be viewed as pretty nasty because people would not have tolerance for any decline in the unemployment rate from levels that are already viewed as representing full employment," he said.
The employment report is due to be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, February 7.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
